clue.text: His car involved self-sacrifice

parts.note: points to the Hindu god Jagannath, whose huge festival chariot devotees were said to throw themselves beneath

explanation.surface: Someone's motoring ended in an act of martyrdom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Car' here is a chariot: the wagon of Jagannath at Puri, under whose wheels pilgrims were reputed to sacrifice themselves, gave English the word for a crushing force.
explanation.definitionFit: The deity of Puri carried on a vast processional wagon is the origin of the English word, so 'his car' is the god's chariot.

clue.text: Every man on the bowling green ?

definitions.meaning: the phrase 'every man ...' means every single person
in lawn bowls the small white target ball has this name

explanation.surface: A question about everyone at the bowls club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every man jack' means everybody; in bowls the small ball everyone aims at is the jack.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'every man ...' completes the first, and the target ball in lawn bowls is the second.

clue.text: Its citizens were not to be told of Saul's death

definitions.text: Its citizens were not to be told of Saul's death

parts.words: Its citizens were not to be told of Saul's death
parts.note: David's lament in 2 Samuel says 'Tell it not in ...', naming a Philistine city

explanation.surface: A town is kept in the dark about the death of a king.
explanation.walkthrough: David's lament for Saul (2 Samuel 1:20) begins 'Tell it not in Gath', so the Philistines would not rejoice.
explanation.definitionFit: The Philistine city named in David's lament was to be kept ignorant of the king's fall.

clue.text: For tendency to get worked up, a moist lemon concoction-about one

indicators.note: the mixed letters go round the following piece
a concoction is a mixture, so the letters of the phrase are mixed up

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A drink made from a lemon gets someone excited.
explanation.walkthrough: AMOISTLEMON is rearranged ('concoction'), and 'about' puts it round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive display of feeling is the habit of being readily stirred.

clue.text: Northern vessel is not so old

parts.note: a ewer is a large jug

explanation.surface: A ship from the north is more modern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship; it is a jug.
explanation.definitionFit: Something less aged is more recent.

clue.text: A French work put here without any objections

parts.note: un is French for a
OP is short for opus, a work
posed means placed or set down in position

explanation.surface: A French play is staged with no complaints.
explanation.walkthrough: UN is the French for 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: With nobody standing against it, a motion passes unchallenged.

clue.text: Bustard lyrically and regretfully "missed '

definitions.meaning: the great bustard's scientific genus name is ...
the Cole Porter song 'Miss ... Regrets' (she's unable to lunch today)

explanation.surface: A large bird is mourned in song.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading needs the Cole Porter song title 'Miss Otis Regrets': in the lyric she sends her apologies, so she is 'missed' with regret.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornithologists file the bustards under that Latin genus, and the song's heroine bears the same surname.

clue.text: They're extremely handy for sketching

parts.note: extremely handy means at the very ends of the hands, and a small rough drawing is named after them

explanation.surface: Some tools are very useful to an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely handy' means at the extremities of the hand, and a quick small drawing is a thumbnail sketch.
explanation.definitionFit: Small quick drawings are called thumbnail sketches, and the nails sit at the tips of the hand.

clue.text: Some beef-about dark clouds perhaps? But look here!

definitions.meaning: a cut of beef from the outer side of the round

definitions.text: about dark clouds perhaps? But look here!
definitions.meaning: every cloud has a silver lining, so there is a brighter face to it worth looking at

explanation.surface: A complaint about gloomy weather, with an appeal to look on the bright side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beef' could mean a grievance; it is meat. The second half recalls 'every cloud has a silver lining': look at its silver side.
explanation.definitionFit: Silverside is a British cut of beef from the hindquarter, and a cloud's bright lining is its silver face.

clue.text: The swab's out of gin

parts.note: the gin is the cotton gin, the machine that separates fibre from seeds, not the spirit

explanation.surface: A sailor or a medical dressing has run dry of spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin' wants to be the drink; it is Eli Whitney's cotton gin, and 'out of' means produced by it. A swab is a wad of the fluffy material.
explanation.definitionFit: A swab is made of the soft fibrous wadding that comes out of the cotton-cleaning machine.

clue.text: Warm drink in the Hebrides

definitions.meaning: to heat wine or ale with spices is to prepare it this way
an island of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys a hot toddy on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hebrides are the island groups off Scotland's west coast; Mull is one of the larger Inner Hebrides.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to heat and spice a beverage, and the same name belongs to a Scottish island.

clue.text: Nodding after rest disturbed by sneezing

indicators.note: the nodding word is placed after the jumbled one
the word rest is disturbed, its letters jumbled

parts.note: nutation is a nodding motion of the head

explanation.surface: Someone dozing after a rest is woken by a sneeze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nodding' looks like dozing off, but nutation is the technical word for a nodding movement; 'disturbed' jumbles the rest, and 'after' sets the nodding piece behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: The formal medical term for a sneeze comes from Latin sternuere.

clue.text: " Belt up, dear " is possibly said of old Mac

indicators.note: signals that the quoted phrase and the word after it might be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A rude remark to a Scotsman called Mac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mac' looks like a Scotsman's name; it is a mackintosh, a raincoat. BELTUPDEAR plus IS is shuffled by 'possibly'. A shabby old raincoat is not respectable.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattered old raincoat is scruffy and of poor repute, the adjective used of shabby clothing.

clue.text: To make merely a thousand in a depression needs some fixing

indicators.note: the first pieces go inside the depression

parts.note: a dent is a hollow
just means merely
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Making only a thousand while in a slump calls for some repair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is the container signal: merely-plus-a-thousand sits inside the depression, with 'a' before it. 'To make' and 'needs' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A small correction or tweak is a piece of repair work.

clue.text: Malthus warned of its explosive force

definitions.text: Malthus warned of its explosive force

parts.words: Malthus warned of its explosive force
parts.note: Thomas Malthus argued that the number of people grows faster than food supply

explanation.surface: An economist warns about a dangerous bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Explosive' suggests a bomb; the modern phrase is the population explosion that Malthus foresaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Malthus's essay predicted that human numbers would outgrow food supply.

clue.text: They're proverbially late-hammered at the entrance

definitions.text: They're proverbially late-hammered at the entrance

parts.words: They're proverbially late-hammered at the entrance
parts.note: late means dead, as in the saying about something as dead as an iron stud driven into a door

explanation.surface: Latecomers arrive drunk at the front door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' and 'hammered' suggest tardy drunks; 'late' means dead, as in 'dead as a doornail', and these studs are literally hammered into the entrance door.
explanation.definitionFit: Large-headed studs knocked into old doors are the subject of the saying 'dead as a ...'.

clue.text: In testy mood, king-emperor rises and falls overboard

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read from bottom to top

parts.note: RI stands for Rex Imperator, king and emperor
RI again, this time read downwards as it falls
board means table, and 'over' says in this down clue that the king pieces sit above it

explanation.surface: An irascible monarch storms about and goes over the side of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: RI (Rex Imperator) 'rises' upwards as IR, then 'falls' downwards as RI; 'over' sets them above TABLE ('board').
explanation.definitionFit: Being short-tempered is the same as being easily annoyed.

clue.text: He has left here a manuscript of considerable length

indicators.note: the word He has gone out of the following word, so those letters are deleted

explanation.surface: A man has gone, leaving behind a long handwritten document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He has left here' tells you to take HE out of HERE, leaving RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Paper is sold by the ream, so writing at great length is said to run to them.

clue.text: It's habitually drunk

parts.note: a regular at a pub orders the same drink every time

explanation.surface: Someone is described as a chronic drunkard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' reads as an inebriated person; it is the past participle, the drink a regular always has, ordered as 'the usual'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub regular's standing order is called by the barman 'the same as ever', the customary one.

clue.text: Ono heart thus makes the game

definitions.text: Ono heart thus makes the game

parts.words: Ono heart thus makes the game
parts.note: in contract bridge, a one-heart bid doubled and then doubled back again scores enough for game

explanation.surface: A lover's single heart wins the match.
explanation.walkthrough: This is bridge: a contract of one heart that is doubled and then redoubled earns enough points to make game.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge, doubling an opponent's double raises the score fourfold, enough for a one-level contract to reach game.

clue.text: Crossing to the island needs money — this stage is in between

parts.note: transit means passage or crossing
Iona is the small Hebridean island of St Columba
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A ferry trip to an island has to be paid for.
explanation.walkthrough: IONA is the small Scottish island where St Columba founded his monastery. L (pound) is a common abbreviation for money.
explanation.definitionFit: A passing phase between two states is described as an intermediate one.

clue.text: Nothing is as confusing as its mirage

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: the two short words are confused, their letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller is bewildered by a vision in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confusing' rearranges IS AS into ASIS after O. A desert mirage typically shows a watering place.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage seen in the desert is classically of a green watering hole.

clue.text: Stake one's fortune ?

definitions.meaning: a post driven into the ground
to make one's ... is to make a fortune

explanation.surface: A gambler bets everything they own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stake' looks like a bet; it is a wooden post. 'Make one's pile' means get rich.
explanation.definitionFit: A driven post supports a building, and a large accumulated sum of money is also called this.

clue.text: One of them is an escapee from the pen

definitions.text: One of them is an escapee from the pen

parts.words: One of them is an escapee from the pen
parts.note: pen is a writing instrument, not a prison or animal enclosure

explanation.surface: A convict breaks out of jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a prison; it is a fountain pen, and what runs out of it is writing fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: The coloured fluids that flow from a fountain pen are its writing liquids.

clue.text: The picture palace features it

indicators.note: the opening words contain the run of letters that is wanted, as a cinema would put a film on its bill

explanation.surface: A cinema puts on a big film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picture palace' is an old British term for a cinema, which might show a grand historical film.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand historical film is the sort of big feature an old cinema would screen.

clue.text: The bottomless pit in one, by an African

parts.note: the abyss is the bottomless pit of scripture
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grim description of a deep hole, involving someone from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' simply places the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Abyssinia is the old name for Ethiopia, so a native of that country is from that continent.

clue.text: Wine in which we see purpose

definitions.meaning: a deep red Spanish wine used as communion wine
a canvas shelter is a place where we may see things, and putting IN before the word gives a synonym for purpose

explanation.surface: A drink reveals someone's aim.
explanation.walkthrough: Tent is an old name for a dark red Spanish wine. The second half plays on 'in tent', which sounds like intent, or purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish red communion wine has this name, and a camping shelter is a place in which one sits and sees.

clue.text: Mercury and Haigha for instance

parts.note: two examples of envoys: the Roman gods' herald and the March Hare's counterpart in Through the Looking-Glass

explanation.surface: A planet and a strange name are listed together.
explanation.walkthrough: Mercury carried the messages of the Roman gods; Haigha is one of the King's two Anglo-Saxon couriers in Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Both figures are bearers of news: one for the gods of Rome, one for Carroll's White King.
